title: Eclipse of Thales (battle of the Lydians and Medes)
summary: Herodotus reports that a battle between the Lydians and the Medes ended when day suddenly turned to night, an event Thales of Miletus had publicly foretold to the Ionians. Many modern historians identify it with the total solar eclipse of 28 May 585 BCE, but the dating and the prediction itself are debated.

uncertainty.note: The 585 BCE identification is the mainstream one but is argued over. The Worthen paper also discusses eclipses of 30 September 610 and 18 May 603 as alternatives visible from Asia Minor, so the range runs back to 610 BCE (astronomical -609).

as_recorded.value: a total eclipse visible in the Aegean and Asia Minor on 28 May 585
On May 28, 585 BCE, a solar eclipse ended a six-year war.

where.modern_name: Kızılırmak (ancient Halys) river, Turkey; the battlefield is not located
where.historical_name: The Halys River, where the Lydians and Medes fought

importance.justification: Often cited as one of the oldest events in the Greek world with a date fixed by astronomy, and as an early claim of an eclipse prediction.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the pin: sources place the battle only "along the Halys River" and the battlefield is unknown, so the pin is the Wikidata point for the Kızılırmak with a 400 km uncertainty. That Wikidata point lies in the eastern part of the river, far from the likely front. The 585 BCE date is the usual identification, not settled; the prediction by Thales rests on Herodotus.
